beta_new: The route begins from camp at 3,000 ft on the North Fork Nooksack River and ascends via a reconnoitered route to reach the bergschrund at 6,500 ft. From there, climbers kick steps up an 800-foot, 50-degree ice couloir on the north face, then traverse westward into a rock trough before tackling the final 1,200 feet of fourth-class rock climbing along the north arête to the summit.

Shares the North Face's first pitch from the notch, then on pitch 2 continues up and right to a prominent vertical crack before traversing left across the face to a large boulder — a long, wandering pitch prone to rope drag. The final pitch climbs a bolted ramp up and left to the summit. Slightly harder and more sustained than the standard North Face.

The couloir has been climbed on foot (crampons) and descended on skis; above the couloir, roughly 800 vertical feet of dry, loose talus on the north ridge leads to the summit. A 2024 ascent found the snow "shockingly icy" and bypassed part of the slope by dropping right onto loose rock and scree.

moves.from: From the Cedar Creek Trail, parties leave the trail to bushwhack toward Cedar Creek, ford it (difficulty varies greatly with flow — see Watch Out), and continue cross-country along/above the Shelokum Creek drainage to open terrain below a broad, moderately angled northwest couloir.

beta_new: From a backcountry camp at Gardner Meadows (or, for a combined trip with Gardner Mountain, a high bivy near Point 8487), climbers work up scree and talus into the bowl below Point 8487, then make an exposed but sub-Class-3 traverse across to the North Gardner summit block. The line is entirely off-trail cross-country travel with no fixed protection, no established cairned route, and route-finding around cliff bands required. Most parties combine it with Gardner Mountain in a single overnight or two-night trip.

From a camp at Whatcom Pass (5,210 ft), head directly south on climbers' trail/talus toward the peak. The ridge narrows and steepens with elevation; expect steep, 'Eldorado-like' snow fins with real exposure, followed by loose 3rd- and occasionally 4th-class scrambling on generally poor rock near the top. Widely considered the fastest way to the summit from either approach valley.

Starting from the North Ridge Notch, climbers ascend a trough and over unprotected 5.6 slab to gain the ridge crest, then follow 2nd- and 3rd-class ramps and corners favoring the east (left) side of the crest. A short 5.0 downclimb bypasses the final gendarme before a sustained 5.4 pitch up the summit headwall (crux moves can be linked with the final pitch on a 70m rope) finishes at the true summit.

First recorded climbed by Mark Bebie on September 7, 1986, who reached it by descending a couloir onto an unnamed glacier north of Primus (accessed from the North Klawatti Glacier after climbing Austera Peak the same day) and traversing to the ridge's base. The ridge took about an hour to climb once gained. It is very rarely repeated and only lightly documented.

moves.value: Other parties have reached the ridge from McAllister Camp by way of Tricouni Peak's lower north ridge, or by a north-south glacier traverse between Primus and Eldorado.
moves.from: ; other parties have approached instead from McAllister Camp via Tricouni Peak's lower north ridge, or via a north-south Primus-Eldorado glacier traverse

beta_new: Approach as for Forbidden Peak and camp at lower (5,300 ft) or upper (6,400 ft) bivy sites. From camp, navigate toward Forbidden Gully or Cat Scratch Gullies and traverse toward the notch to the right of the North Ridge. Make three to four fourth-class pitches to tower base, then climb the crux 40-foot 5.5 pitch to the tower top. For descent, make one 40-foot rappel and reverse the ridge climb.

The North Ridge - West Side is one of the primary technical routes on Molar Tooth. The route ascends via the west rib with multiple short low 5th class pitches (up to 5.4), solid granite with vertical jointing, though protection is spaced in places, and enjoyable alpine climbing despite loose rock concerns.

moves.from: The descent via north ridge rappels requires careful anchor placement and rope management due to potential loose rock.

beta_new: A ridge-crest link between Cloudy Peak and North Star: from Cloudy Pass, scramble the ridge up to Cloudy Peak with expanding views toward Glacier Peak, Eldorado, and Buckner, on rock that is reasonably solid Class 4 with an option to keep it at Class 3. From Cloudy Peak, lose elevation and cross talus slopes to reach North Star, finishing on the same lichen-slicked Class 3-4 summit step as the standard route.

moves.from: Most parties descend directly toward the Cloudy Pass Trail (rejoining it around 6,300 ft) rather than re-climbing Cloudy Peak.

beta_new: From a camp at Lyman Lakes, leave the trail and hike cross-country across open meadow, then up talus and scree (Class 2) on the south side of the mountain, with the final push to the summit on looser, steeper Class 2-3 rock. The peak is commonly combined with adjacent Cloudy Peak (about 0.9 mi away) from the same basin camp.

A wonderful alpine rock climb with great exposure and views. The route offers generally solid protection with the crux featuring a wide flaring chimney and off-width section requiring careful gear placement. First three pitches establish the ridge; crux pitch (P4) is 5.7-5.8 in a chimney; final pitches are 4th class scrambling to the tower summit.

The West Ridge is the standard and by far the most popular route on North Twin Sister. After a long logging-road and trail approach to treeline near Dailey Prairie, the route follows the ridge crest (keeping to climber's right of the crest on the lower ridge and moving to climber's left near the false summits, to avoid the hardest moves) past two named rock features — the 'Obelisk' and the 'Cockscomb' — with a notch around 6,300 ft that bypasses a cliff band where the crest is blocked. Most of the climbing is class 3 on excellent, high-friction rock with frequent holds; a handful of class 4 (and, on the crest itself, occasional class 5) moves are encountered, and some parties rope up for a short M1b mixed step on a variation start. Multiple false summits complicate routefinding near the top.

moves.from: Descent is either back down the ridge or, early season, a steep glissade down snow on the north face.

beta_new: Lower pitches climb a rubble-covered class 4 gully into a snow couloir that steepens past 65 degrees with overhanging chalkstones near its top; the crux is two 5.6 pitches around the 'duolith,' a loose 30-foot granite tower split by a 3-foot crack, climbed on sparse protection (one 80-meter pitch protected by a single piece) before easier class 3-4 terrain leads up the north ridge crest to the summit.

Grade: 5.7+ YDS, Grade IV, 12 pitches, 4,000 feet. First ascent: 1963. Route: Climb partway up C-J couloir to hanging glacier on right; ascend leftmost rib to summit. Hazards: Objective danger from falling rock/ice, steep snow, exposed scrambling, avalanche potential. Best season: July-September. No bush climbing.

moves.from: Equipment: Small-to-medium alpine rock rack (to 3 inches), 10+ runners, helmet.

beta_new: A squeeze chimney and friction slab low on the route lead to a well-protected layback/jam crack for the standout second pitch, followed by flared corner-crack systems and a final stemming open-book/gully pitch to third-class terrain just below the summit. Several sections are rated R for sparse protection, so this is a more serious Grade II than the rating alone suggests.

P1 is a committing traverse and corner (~10 hard moves) to a ledge belay; P2 is a right-facing corner with limited feet and hard gear placement (5.11a); P3 is a chimney then vegetated crack over a block (~5.8); P4 is a scramble approach to the overhangs; P5 pulls a pair of obvious overhangs with good protection (~5.10); P6 finishes with hand-crack climbing to the summit (~5.9).

From the Redoubt Glacier saddle (high camp at 7,150 ft), traverse to the northeast ridge saddle below the col between the twin spires. Climb 2-3 pitches of Class 4-5 rock (crux involves manteling wet slabs) to gain the ridge crest. Continue with Class 3-4 ridge scrambling and occasional low 5th class moves to the summit. Lichen and water seepage make holds unreliable; test all holds before committing weight.

After a long approach across the Inspiration and McAllister Glaciers, the Northwest Ridge offers three short (each well under 25 m/rope-length), moderate pitches to the summit — the easiest established route on the peak, popular as a descent for other routes.

This ridge was first climbed in 2018 as one leg of the 'Boston Marathon' — a ~26.2-mile, mostly-soloed technical traverse circling the entire rim of Boston Basin (26 pitches up to 5.8 R, 26 rappels, 20,000+ ft of technical terrain). The ridge itself is deep, virgin choss rated 5.5 X, including a two-pitch section climbed à cheval (straddling the ridge crest) across rock with the consistency of feta cheese, followed by roughly 1,000 additional feet of similarly poor climbing. It is accessed along the basin rim from the direction of Sharkfin Tower. There is no established description of this specific ridge as an independent route — treat it as an obscure, rarely-repeated line rather than a maintained trade route.

Shares P1 and P2 with the standard Northwest Face. On P3, rather than the 5.8+ flakes pitch to the right, climb a well-protected crack trending slightly left (5.7) for ~40 ft, place a final solid 1-2" piece where the crack narrows, then continue up a 5.10 flared groove past two bolts and tricky slab to the belay ledge. P4-5 rejoin the standard Northwest Face to the west summit.

The Northwest Ridge is the moderate line on Colchuck Balanced Rock and the route of choice for parties who want the summit rather than the west face's hard free climbing. The line gains an obvious gully from Colchuck Lake to the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, then third-class terrain leading to the ridge proper, followed by the sharp ridge at 5.6 to the summit. Total gain from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to the summit is about 4,760 ft, and a relaxed car-to-car time is roughly 12 hours. The final obstacle is the balanced summit block itself, a short boulder problem that most parties protect. The rock is granodiorite. The peak's first ascent was made in 1958 by Gene Prater and Thomas Quin, though not necessarily by this line.

moves.from: Descent from the summit was a single 25 m rappel off an anchor down the east side, then scrambling talus around to the south saddle and back past Jabberwocky Tower to Colchuck Lake.

beta_new: Old Guard is usually tagged as a side-trip from a Ptarmigan Traverse camp near the Le Conte-Sentinel col (roughly 7,300-7,400 ft). From the col, rope up and cross the Le Conte Glacier, skirting crevasses and a bergschrund, to reach a snow ramp on the peak's northwest side. Above the ramp the route eases into a straightforward but somewhat loose, indistinct class 2-3 rock scramble to the summit. Most parties climb neighboring Sentinel Peak from the same camp in the same outing.

From the PCT's high point, leave it on an unsigned boot path that switchbacks up scree/talus to the northwest ridge and follows it south to the summit; the last ~50 feet is loose Class 2–3 rock with real but manageable exposure. An alternate line gains the col between Old Snowy and Ives Peak and follows the ridge crest/just-south-of-crest to the top.

moves.from: From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead, hike ~5.4 miles through forest and meadows to the PCT, then follow the PCT north/west around the mountain's flank to its high point.

beta_new: Approach the summit block from the north side (from Snow Dome and/or Crystal Pass traverse), then climb directly up the North Face instead of via the East Face ramps or northwest edge. This line is steeper and more exposed, with Class 5.4 climbing throughout.

After reaching the base of the summit block (via any approach), this variation climbs the northwestern edge of the block directly. The rock is generally more solid than the East Face, with several Class 5.3-5.4 moves. The exposure is significant but the climbing is more straightforward.

After summiting the West Peak via the standard Blue Glacier route or a variation, descend to the saddle between West and Middle Peaks (this descent is not technical but involves careful route-finding and downclimbing). Cross to Middle Peak (7,929 feet), which has Class 3-4 scrambling. Continue to East Peak (7,762 feet) with additional Class 3-4 scrambling and potential crevassed terrain. Reverse the approach from the East Peak to descend back to Glacier Meadows via an alternative glacier system or retrace the standard route.

Begins on blocky terrain at the downhill (toward-the-hairpin) end of the wall. Above the scrambly start the rock looks deceptively low-angle; scramble the lower section and trend right as it steepens, aiming for the arete after a short, exposed rightward traverse. Continue up varied knobs, crimps, and jugs. Near the top, traverse left on bolts through steeper, similarly-featured climbing to the anchors — the position and quality of climbing are better than the route looks from the ground, though the bolts themselves can be hard to spot before starting.
Starts at two wide, left-leaning cracks about 50 ft right of the base of the Classic Route; climbs up and left toward the shared anchors (block with tat and rings) used by The Roof.

From a camp at Lake Doris (6,975 ft), leave the trail and head roughly northeast through open forest for about 0.6 mile, then climb the long southwest-facing talus slope, gaining about 1,400 ft to the southwest ridge/south face before finishing to the summit (8,587 ft). Terrain is Class 2 throughout: loose scree low down giving way to talus and boulders higher up. A faint climber's path along the southwest ridge is reported to be easier going than a direct line up the boulder-strewn south face. As a climb from the south the peak is a long, tedious talus slog, while more involved, chossy climbing exists on the unfrequented east and north sides, which are not part of this standard route.

From the Otto-Himmel Col (reached via Stump Hollow trail from Goodell Creek trailhead), ascend the east ridge directly to the summit. Early season (June–July): route is primarily snow with Class II-III scrambling near summit; descent is straightforward on consolidated snow. Mid-season (July–August): snow transitions to exposed rock; negotiable as Class III with careful foot placement. Late season (August–September): loose, tricky 5th class scrambling through chossy rock and talus fields. Final approach to summit features a fresh rockfall zone approximately 30 feet below summit ridge; experienced alpinists rope-protect the 5.7 pitches or navigate unstable terrain carefully. Route is approximately 500–700 vertical feet from col to summit.

There is no single defined 'route' up Oval Peak so much as a set of interchangeable Class 2 ridge/slope lines that all converge near the summit. Parties commonly approach via the West Fork Buttermilk Trail No. 411 or the Oval Creek Trail No. 410A/Eagle Creek Trail, leave the trail in the basin below the peak, and climb whichever ridge (east, southwest, or south) looks cleanest that day, often descending a different one for better scree/talus conditions. The peak is defined by talus — talus, talus, and more talus — with large boulders higher up. A popular variation links Oval with neighboring Star and Courtney Peaks via the Fish Creek Pass / West Buttermilk Ridge traverse.
Ascend the glacier, navigate crevasses and moats, then climb the exposed fourth class rock on the northeast side of the summit pyramid. Crampons and ice tools are essential.

moves.value: Another way in follows the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River trail to Dutch Miller Gap, then bushwhacks to a basecamp at Overcoat Lake and contours over to the Overcoat Glacier.
moves.from: Approach via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River trail to Dutch Miller Gap, then bushwhack to Overcoat Lake basecamp and contour to the Overcoat Glacier.
Descent is via downclimbing and rappels to return to the glacier.

beta_new: From the North Fork Sauk trailhead, hike the maintained Red Mountain Trail (signed 'Painted Mountain Lookout Trail') about 1 mile to its end near the old 1936-67 lookout site (~2,800 ft). Ascend roughly 70 vertical feet of steep, moss-and-dirt-covered rock ledges (Class 3, exposed in spots) to gain the southwest ridge. From there a faint boot path, sometimes marked with pink flagging, climbs open meadows and rock along the ridge/shoulder to an overlook of Ruby Lake near 5,800 ft, then continues on steeper ground to about 6,700 ft before scree slopes lead to the 6,975 ft summit. The whole outing (car-to-car) is roughly 8 miles round trip with about 4,875 ft of total elevation gain.

From the summit of Painted Mountain, follow the crest east over broken ridge and snowfields to Magenta Peak. The section from Magenta to Black Mountain is the crux: the ridge is cut by numerous gendarmes that push you off the crest to find bypasses, with at least one awkward mossy downclimb. Black Mountain, the high point of the route, has several ways up: loose scree gullies on its southeast side; a steep heather chute from the basin on its south side to a small col just west of the summit block, then a short, exposed class 3 scramble up the northwest ridge; or, harder, a class 4 corner with slabby footholds on the north side. Descend Black's south side, over lingering snow early in the season, into the basin below it toward Brown Peak, whose summit can be skipped by crossing its shoulder. Continue south to the base of Skullcap Peak and tag it, then follow easier ridge with decent use paths over the Purple Peak area to Portal Peak. Drop to Red Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail and follow the crest to White Mountain, whose south ridge has a climber's path.

A thin crux comes in the first couple of bolts, with the third bolt set higher than ideal due to hollow rock near that stance. Above this, the climbing eases with slightly spaced bolts leading to the top of the wall.

Pernod and neighboring Chablis are the easiest of the Wine Spires, and this line is a reasonable day from a Burgundy Col camp. The climbing is moderate (about 5.5-5.7) and not sustained. It climbs from the east side up to the notch between Pernod and Chianti and then up the northeast corner to a tiny summit block; the South Face and the Direct West Face are separate, harder routes on the same spire.

The standard approach to Phantom Peak uses the Southwest Glacier and South Couloir with a snow ramp at approximately 40-45 degrees. Climbers cross a bergschrund, navigate a steep snow finger, then move onto broken rock with Class 2-3 scrambling before traversing the sharp, exposed summit ridge. The summit consists of solid granitic rock with thrilling exposure on both sides. A hand line or belay may be useful for the narrowest sections.

Pinnacle's standard route gains the peak's west-southwest scree-and-talus facade (the gentle side, opposite the precipitous, largely unclimbed east face). Most parties backpack in 9-13 miles through the North Fork Entiat/Snow Brushy Creek drainage to a high basin camp near Saska Pass, then day-trip the summit by dropping into Snow Brushy Creek and climbing to the crest saddle just south of the peak. The final roughly 800 ft to the top is unroped class 2-3 scree and ridge scrambling with no technical climbing; it is very commonly combined with nearby Saska Peak and/or Emerald Peak from the same camp.

From Pinnacle-Plummer saddle, head east and scramble up obvious gullies on the peak's south side with multiple line options. Stay on most-traveled route for least loose rock. Route-finding is straightforward but exposure increases with altitude. Final push to summit is the steepest and most difficult section, with some variations described as low 5th class.

The usual line is the obvious chute just east of the peak's westernmost rock prominence, about a quarter mile along the boot path from the saddle toward the west side of the south face. Reach it over scree and loose rock along or below the ridge. The chute gets steeper and more exposed as it climbs, but the rock is better cleaned higher up. Protection is limited to a few horns and trees near the top that can be slung, and some parties back off the short top step on one.
